claim: Mice with adenine-induced CKD develop inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting similar to patients with CKD.
source: Here, we report that similar to patients with CKD, mice with adenine-induced CKD develop inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Mice fed high phosphate diet develop inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting even without CKD.
source: These complications are also observed in mice fed high phosphate diet even without CKD.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Ablation of pathologic FGF23-FGFR4 signaling did not protect mice on an increased phosphate diet from inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting.
source: Ablation of pathologic FGF23-FGFR4 signaling did not protect mice on an increased phosphate diet or mice with adenine-induced CKD from these sequelae.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on experimental observations using FGFR4 knockout mice.

claim: Ablation of pathologic FGF23-FGFR4 signaling did not protect mice with adenine-induced CKD from inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting.
source: Ablation of pathologic FGF23-FGFR4 signaling did not protect mice on an increased phosphate diet or mice with adenine-induced CKD from these sequelae.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on experimental observations using FGFR4 knockout mice.

claim: Low phosphate diet ameliorated anemia and skeletal muscle wasting in a genetic mouse model of CKD.
source: However, low phosphate diet ameliorated anemia and skeletal muscle wasting in a genetic mouse model of CKD.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on experimental observations in Alport mice.

claim: Phosphate elevations induce inflammatory signaling in hepatocytes.
source: Our mechanistic in vitro studies indicate that phosphate elevations induce inflammatory signaling and increase hepcidin expression in hepatocytes, a potential causative link between hyperphosphatemia, anemia, and skeletal muscle dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on in vitro experiments with primary hepatocytes.

claim: Phosphate elevations increase hepcidin expression in hepatocytes.
source: Our mechanistic in vitro studies indicate that phosphate elevations induce inflammatory signaling and increase hepcidin expression in hepatocytes, a potential causative link between hyperphosphatemia, anemia, and skeletal muscle dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding in the abstract based on in vitro experiments with primary hepatocytes.

claim: High phosphate intake from consumption of processed food may have harmful effects irrespective of pre-existing kidney injury.
source: Our study suggests that high phosphate intake, as caused by the consumption of processed food, may have harmful effects irrespective of pre-existing kidney injury, supporting not only the clinical utility of treating hyperphosphatemia in CKD patients but also arguing for limiting phosphate intake in healthy individuals.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion based on the study findings, representing an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Phosphate is an essential mineral nutrient.
source: Phosphate (Pi) is an essential mineral nutrient (Erem and Razzaque, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established fact.

claim: FGF23 is the chief hormone maintaining body Pi balance by promoting renal Pi excretion when Pi load is high.
source: Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) is the chief hormone maintaining body Pi balance by promoting renal Pi excretion when Pi load is high (Fukumoto and Yamashita, 2007; Isakova et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this established fact about FGF23 function.

claim: Hyperphosphatemic states can result from rare genetic disorders such as familial tumoral calcinosis.
source: Hyperphosphatemic states can result from various conditions, including rare genetic disorders, such as familial tumoral calcinosis (FTC), and acquired diseases, such as chronic kidney disease (CKD), which are more frequent.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about causes of hyperphosphatemia.

claim: Hyperphosphatemic states can result from chronic kidney disease.
source: Hyperphosphatemic states can result from various conditions, including rare genetic disorders, such as familial tumoral calcinosis (FTC), and acquired diseases, such as chronic kidney disease (CKD), which are more frequent.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about causes of hyperphosphatemia.

claim: Increased consumption of foods and drinks rich in Pi-based additives is expanding in Westernized diets, leading to excess dietary Pi intake.
source: Moreover, increased consumption of foods and drinks rich in Pi-based additives is expanding in Westernized diets, leading to excess dietary Pi intake (Carrigan et al., 2014; Gutiérrez et al., 2010a).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about dietary trends.

claim: CKD patients have an increased risk of death that is attributable to complications such as inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting.
source: CKD patients have an increased risk of death that is attributable to complications such as inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting (Amdur et al., 2016; Hoshino et al., 2020; Stenvinkel et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this clinical observation.

claim: The etiology of CKD-associated anemia is multifactorial and includes absolute iron deficiency and functional iron deficiency.
source: The etiology of CKD-associated anemia is multifactorial and includes absolute iron deficiency and functional iron deficiency, with the latter caused by inflammatory cytokines including interleukin-6 (IL6) and interleukin-1β (IL1β).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about CKD-associated anemia.

claim: Functional iron deficiency in CKD is caused by inflammatory cytokines including interleukin-6 (IL6) and interleukin-1β (IL1β).
source: The etiology of CKD-associated anemia is multifactorial and includes absolute iron deficiency and functional iron deficiency, with the latter caused by inflammatory cytokines including interleukin-6 (IL6) and interleukin-1β (IL1β).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about the mechanism of functional iron deficiency.

claim: Inflammatory mediators IL6 and IL1β can directly induce the release of the liver-hormone hepcidin.
source: These inflammatory mediators can directly induce the release of the liver-hormone hepcidin, the master regulator of iron metabolism (Verga Falzacappa et al., 2007; Ganz and Nemeth, 2012; Kanamori et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this mechanism.

claim: Hepcidin is the master regulator of iron metabolism.
source: These inflammatory mediators can directly induce the release of the liver-hormone hepcidin, the master regulator of iron metabolism (Verga Falzacappa et al., 2007; Ganz and Nemeth, 2012; Kanamori et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this established fact about hepcidin function.

claim: Hepcidin controls the flow of iron into circulation by regulating the iron exporter ferroportin (FPN).
source: Hepcidin controls the flow of iron into circulation by regulating the iron exporter ferroportin (FPN) (Nemeth et al., 2004b).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this mechanism of hepcidin action.

claim: Hepcidin binding occludes FPN and induces its degradation.
source: Hepcidin binding occludes FPN (Aschemeyer et al., 2018; Billesbølle et al., 2020) and induces its degradation, thereby restricting iron efflux into the circulation from iron recycling macrophages, a process also known as reticuloendothelial system (RES) blockade, and from duodenal enterocytes responsible for dietary iron absorption.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this molecular mechanism.

claim: Hepcidin-induced FPN degradation restricts iron efflux from iron recycling macrophages (RES blockade) and duodenal enterocytes.
source: Hepcidin binding occludes FPN (Aschemeyer et al., 2018; Billesbølle et al., 2020) and induces its degradation, thereby restricting iron efflux into the circulation from iron recycling macrophages, a process also known as reticuloendothelial system (RES) blockade, and from duodenal enterocytes responsible for dietary iron absorption.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about the consequences of hepcidin action.

claim: Hepcidin-mediated iron restriction reduces serum iron levels (hypoferremia), limiting the supply of iron for erythrocyte production.
source: Collectively, these events reduce serum iron levels (hypoferremia), limiting the supply of iron for erythrocyte production (Nemeth et al., 2004a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this consequence of hepcidin action.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines such as IL6 and IL1β act on skeletal muscle and induce muscle wasting.
source: Inflammatory cytokines such as IL6 and IL1β also act on skeletal muscle and induce muscle wasting, a comorbidity affecting 65% of CKD patients (Kovesdy et al., 2013; Li et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this mechanism of muscle wasting.

claim: Muscle wasting is a comorbidity affecting 65% of CKD patients.
source: Inflammatory cytokines such as IL6 and IL1β also act on skeletal muscle and induce muscle wasting, a comorbidity affecting 65% of CKD patients (Kovesdy et al., 2013; Li et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this clinical statistic.

claim: The loss of protein from muscle is ascribed to protein degradation by the ubiquitin–proteasome system, suppression of protein synthesis and impaired growth of new muscle fibers.
source: The loss of protein from muscle is ascribed to protein degradation by the ubiquitin–proteasome system, suppression of protein synthesis and impaired growth of new muscle fibers (Wang and Mitch, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this mechanism of muscle protein loss.

claim: Pleotropic activities of IL6 and IL1β induce the production of myostatin, a pivotal mediator of skeletal muscle wasting.
source: As pleotropic activities of IL6 and IL1β induce the production of myostatin, a pivotal mediator of skeletal muscle wasting, these actions foster the simultaneous induction of atrophy-related gene programs and reduced cellular responses to progrowth signals, which initiates protein synthesis suppression.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about the mechanism linking inflammation to muscle wasting.

claim: Inflammation and myostatin advance CKD-associated comorbidities which reduce the survival and quality of life of CKD patients.
source: Together, inflammation and myostatin advance these CKD-associated comorbidities which reduce the survival and quality of life of CKD patients (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this clinical consequence.

claim: Hyperphosphatemia and excess serum FGF23 are factors associated with inflammation, anemia, and mortality in CKD.
source: A prominent aspect of CKD is altered mineral metabolism, where hyperphosphatemia and excess serum FGF23 are factors associated with inflammation, anemia, and mortality (Mehta et al., 2017; Munoz Mendoza et al., 2017; Navarro-González et al., 2009; Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support these clinical associations.

claim: Studies of the effects of dietary Pi restriction in animal models are scarce.
source: Studies of the effects of dietary Pi restriction in animal models are scarce.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an observation about the current state of research.

claim: Dietary interventions to lower Pi intake are challenging because they require long-term behavioral changes made more difficult by the lack of disclosure of Pi content of foods and beverages by the food industry.
source: Dietary interventions to lower Pi intake are challenging because they require long-term behavioral changes made more difficult by the lack of disclosure of Pi content of foods and beverages by the food industry (Gutiérrez and Wolf, 2010b).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this statement about challenges in dietary interventions.

claim: Type III Na/Pi cotransporters, PiT-1 and PiT-2, are ubiquitously expressed and mediate cellular Pi homeostasis in all cells.
source: Type III Na/Pi cotransporters, PiT-1 and PiT-2, are ubiquitously expressed and mediate cellular Pi homeostasis in all cells (Lederer and Miyamoto, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established fact about PiT-1 and PiT-2 function.

claim: Pathologic Pi accumulation in vasculature is mediated by PiT-1 and PiT-2, loading Pi into vascular smooth muscle cells where it activates signaling networks such as Ras/MAPK and NFκB.
source: Pathologic Pi accumulation in vasculature is mediated by PiT-1 and PiT-2, loading Pi into vascular smooth muscle cells where it activates signaling networks such as Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NFκB) (Chavkin et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this mechanism of Pi-induced vascular pathology.

claim: Under physiologic conditions, bone-derived FGF23 targets the kidney to increase Pi excretion by activating its canonical signaling complex, FGFR1 and co-receptor Klotho.
source: Under physiologic conditions, bone-derived FGF23 targets the kidney to increase Pi excretion by activating its canonical signaling complex, fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) and co-receptor Klotho (Czaya and Faul, 2019a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this established mechanism of FGF23 action.

claim: When FGF23 is in pathological excess, increased FGF23 targets the heart and liver by activating FGFR4, independently of Klotho.
source: When FGF23 is in pathological excess, as found in dietary Pi overload or CKD, increased FGF23 targets the heart and liver by activating FGFR4, independently of Klotho (Faul et al., 2011; Grabner et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this mechanism of pathologic FGF23 action.

claim: The noncanonical FGF23-FGFR4 mechanism recruits FGFR4 as a pathologic receptor mediating the effects of excess FGF23 to cause cardiac hypertrophy and promote inflammation.
source: This noncanonical mechanism recruits FGFR4 as a pathologic receptor mediating the effects of excess FGF23 to cause cardiac hypertrophy and promote inflammation (Faul et al., 2011; Grabner et al., 2015; Han et al., 2020; Leifheit-Nestler et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this pathologic mechanism.

claim: Following adenine diet for 14 weeks, Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice displayed comparable renal dysfunction, as shown by elevations in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine levels.
source: Following adenine diet for 14 weeks, Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice displayed comparable renal dysfunction, as shown by elevations in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1A showing the data.

claim: On adenine diet, serum FGF23 and Pi levels significantly increased in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− genotypes.
source: On adenine diet, serum FGF23 and Pi levels significantly increased in both genotypes (Figure 1B), as expected with marked kidney injury.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1B showing the data.

claim: No significant changes in serum calcium levels were observed between genotypes on adenine diet despite increased serum Pi levels.
source: No significant changes in serum calcium levels were observed between genotypes on adenine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), despite increased serum Pi levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure data.

claim: Liver IL1β (Il1b), IL6 (Il6), and serum amyloid A1 (Saa1) transcript levels were significantly and similarly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on adenine diet.
source: Unlike in healthy control mice, liver IL1β (Il1b), IL6 (Il6), and serum amyloid A1 (Saa1) transcript levels were significantly and similarly elevated (Figure 1C, D) in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1C and 1D showing the data.

claim: Liver hepcidin (Hamp) mRNA levels were significantly and similarly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on adenine diet.
source: Compared with control mice, Hamp transcript levels were significantly and similarly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on adenine (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1E showing the data.

claim: Complete blood count and serum analyses displayed significant reductions in red blood cell (RBC) count, mean corpuscular volume (MCV), hemoglobin, and serum iron levels on adenine diet.
source: Complete blood count and serum analyses displayed significant reductions in red blood cell (RBC) count, mean corpuscular volume (MCV), hemoglobin, and serum iron levels on adenine diet (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1F showing the data.

claim: Significant reductions in hematocrit percentage (HCT%), mean corpuscular hematocrit (MCH), and serum transferrin saturation percentage (TSAT%) were observed on adenine diet.
source: Significant reductions in hematocrit percentage (HCT%), mean corpuscular hematocrit (MCH), and serum transferrin saturation percentage (TSAT%) were also observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure data.

claim: Spleen tissue sections stained with Perls' Prussian blue revealed profound intracellular iron sequestration in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on adenine, indicating severe RES blockade.
source: Spleen tissue sections stained with Perls' Prussian blue revealed profound intracellular iron sequestration, indicating severe RES blockade in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on adenine (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1G and supplementary figure showing the histological data.

claim: FGF23-FGFR4 signaling does not affect inflammation, the acute phase response or functional iron deficiency and anemia in adenine-induced CKD.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that FGF23-FGFR4 signaling does not affect inflammation, the acute phase response or functional iron deficiency and anemia in adenine-induced CKD.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the comparable findings in wild-type and FGFR4 knockout mice.

claim: Hepatic Pi levels were elevated in both Fgfr4−/− and Fgfr4+/+ mice following adenine diet.
source: Hepatic Pi levels were elevated in both Fgfr4−/− and Fgfr4+/+ mice following adenine (Figure 1H) but less so in Fgfr4−/− mice when compared to Fgfr4+/+ mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1H showing the data.

claim: Hepatic Pi levels were less elevated in Fgfr4−/− mice compared to Fgfr4+/+ mice following adenine diet.
source: Hepatic Pi levels were elevated in both Fgfr4−/− and Fgfr4+/+ mice following adenine (Figure 1H) but less so in Fgfr4−/− mice when compared to Fgfr4+/+ mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1H showing the data.

claim: Serum FGF23 levels increased in both genotypes on 2% Pi and 3% Pi diet, in comparison to mice on 0.7% Pi diet.
source: Serum FGF23 levels increased in both genotypes on 2% Pi and 3% Pi diet, in comparison to mice on 0.7% Pi diet (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A showing the data.

claim: Serum Pi levels significantly increased only on 3% Pi diet, in comparison to mice fed 0.7% Pi diet, despite 2% Pi increasing serum FGF23.
source: Despite 2% Pi increasing serum FGF23, serum Pi levels significantly increased only on 3% Pi, in comparison to mice fed 0.7% Pi (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A showing the data.

claim: No significant differences in serum calcium levels were observed between genotypes on graded phosphate diets despite elevated Pi levels.
source: No significant differences in serum calcium levels were observed between genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), despite elevated Pi levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure data.

claim: No pathologic changes were detected in kidneys of mice on graded phosphate diets as BUN, serum creatinine, and kidney tissue sections stained with H&E appeared similar to those of mice on 0.7% Pi.
source: No pathologic changes were detected in kidneys regardless of genotype as BUN, serum creatinine, and kidney tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) appeared similar to those of mice on 0.7% Pi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: Interstitial fibrosis was not detected in kidneys of mice on graded phosphate diets as shown by Masson's trichrome staining.
source: Interstitial fibrosis was not detected in kidneys as shown by Masson's trichrome staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure showing the histological data.

claim: Elevations in serum levels of FGF23 and Pi in mice on 2% Pi or 3% Pi diet are consequences of an increasing dietary Pi load and not renal dysfunction.
source: These data indicate elevations in serum levels of FGF23 and Pi in mice on 2% Pi or 3% Pi diet are consequences of an increasing dietary Pi load and not renal dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the absence of kidney pathology.

claim: Liver Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 transcript levels significantly increased in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on 3% Pi, although not on 2% Pi diets.
source: Compared to 0.7% Pi, liver Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 transcript levels significantly increased in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice on 3% Pi, although not on 2% Pi diets (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2B and 2C showing the data.

claim: Liver injury was not detected on 3% Pi diet, as no significant elevations in hepatic alanine aminotransferase (Alt1) or aspartate aminotransferase (Ast1) mRNA levels were found.
source: Liver injury was not detected, as no significant elevations in hepatic alanine aminotransferase (Alt1) or aspartate aminotransferase (Ast1) mRNA levels were found on 3% Pi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: Dietary Pi overload induces inflammation, but not via FGF23-FGFR4 signaling.
source: These data support the notion that dietary Pi overload induces inflammation, but not via FGF23-FGFR4 signaling.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the comparable findings in wild-type and FGFR4 knockout mice.

claim: A positive correlation was detected between hepatic and serum Pi levels in both genotypes, beginning with 2% Pi diet.
source: A positive correlation was detected between hepatic and serum Pi levels in both genotypes, beginning with 2% Pi (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2D showing the correlation data.

claim: Liver Pi deposits increase following elevations in dietary Pi content.
source: These results show liver Pi deposits increase following elevations in dietary Pi content.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the correlation between dietary Pi and liver Pi levels.

claim: A positive correlation between liver Pi and liver Hamp mRNA levels were detected in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice, only with diets containing 2% or 3% Pi.
source: A positive correlation between liver Pi and liver Hamp mRNA levels were detected in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice, again only with diets containing 2% or 3% Pi (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2E showing the correlation data.

claim: Elevations in liver Hamp mRNA are independent of liver injury and may result from Pi-driven inflammation.
source: As liver injury was not detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B), these data indicate that elevations in liver Hamp mRNA are independent of liver injury and may result from Pi-driven inflammation.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the absence of liver injury markers and the correlation data.

claim: Marked reductions in RBC, MCV, hemoglobin, and serum iron levels were detected on 3% Pi diet and were similar in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice.
source: Marked reductions in RBC, MCV, hemoglobin, and serum iron levels were detected on 3% Pi and were similar in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2F showing the data.

claim: HCT% and MCH were significantly decreased on 3% Pi diet.
source: HCT% and MCH were also significantly decreased (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure data.

claim: Both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice showed increased intracellular iron deposits in spleen on 3% Pi diet.
source: Supporting these findings, spleen tissue sections revealed that both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice showed increased intracellular iron deposits on 3% Pi (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2G and supplementary figure showing the histological data.

claim: Dietary Pi loading causes iron restriction and hypoferremia even in the absence of CKD.
source: Thus, dietary Pi loading causes iron restriction and hypoferremia even in the absence of CKD.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in mice fed high Pi diet without kidney disease.

claim: Mice on adenine or 3% Pi diet exhibit reduced grip strength in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice, in comparison to respective control mice.
source: Examination of skeletal muscle strength indicates that mice on adenine or 3% Pi diet exhibit reduced grip strength in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice, in comparison to respective control mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3A showing the data.

claim: A reduction in gastrocnemius mass was observed in mice on adenine or 3% Pi diet.
source: A reduction in gastrocnemius mass was also observed (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3B showing the data.

claim: Gastrocnemius metallothionein-1 (Mt1) transcript levels were significantly elevated in both genotypes following adenine and 3% Pi diets.
source: Notably, gastrocnemius metallothionein-1 (Mt1) transcript levels were significantly elevated in both genotypes following adenine and 3% Pi diets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating that either condition fosters skeletal muscle abnormalities.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: Gastrocnemius myostatin (Mstn) transcript levels were significantly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice following adenine or 3% Pi diet.
source: Compared to respective control mice, gastrocnemius myostatin (Mstn) transcript levels were significantly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice following adenine or 3% Pi diet (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3C showing the data.

claim: Both genotypes on 2% Pi showed an increased trend in Mstn mRNA levels.
source: Additionally, both genotypes on 2% Pi showed an increased trend in Mstn mRNA levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3C showing the data.

claim: Gastrocnemius Murf1 and Atrogin1 transcript levels were significantly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice following adenine and 3% Pi diets.
source: Compared with their respective control mice, gastrocnemius Murf1 and Atrogin1 transcript levels were significantly elevated in both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice following adenine and 3% Pi diets (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3D showing the data.

claim: Gastrocnemius tissue sections from Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice, on either adenine or 3% Pi diet, showed smaller muscle fiber size compared with controls.
source: Indeed, gastrocnemius tissue sections stained with H&E from Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice, on either adenine or 3% Pi diet, showed smaller muscle fiber size compared with controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3E showing the histological data.

claim: Skeletal muscle wasting in adenine-induced CKD and hyperphosphatemia does not require FGF23-FGFR4 signaling.
source: Taken together, these data suggest skeletal muscle wasting in adenine-induced CKD and hyperphosphatemia does not require FGF23-FGFR4 signaling.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the comparable findings in wild-type and FGFR4 knockout mice.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice showed renal dysfunction by increased BUN and serum creatinine levels compared to wild-type mice on normal diet.
source: In comparison to wild-type (Col4a3+/+) mice on normal diet (0.6% Pi), Col4a3−/− mice showed renal dysfunction by increased BUN and serum creatinine levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4A showing the data.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice on low Pi diet displayed a reduction in BUN and serum creatinine levels.
source: Col4a3−/− mice on low Pi diet displayed a reduction in both parameters (Figure 4A), along with reduced pathologic alterations in kidney morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4A and supplementary figure showing the data.

claim: Serum levels of FGF23 and Pi significantly increased in Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet compared to wild-type mice.
source: As compared to wild-type mice, serum levels of FGF23 and Pi significantly increased in Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet (Figure 4B), but less so in Col4a3−/− mice on low Pi diet (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4B showing the data.

claim: Serum levels of FGF23 and Pi were less elevated in Col4a3−/− mice on low Pi diet compared to Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet.
source: As compared to wild-type mice, serum levels of FGF23 and Pi significantly increased in Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet (Figure 4B), but less so in Col4a3−/− mice on low Pi diet (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4B showing the data.

claim: Liver Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 transcript levels were significantly elevated in Col4a3−/− mice compared to wild-type mice on normal diet but much less elevated on 0.2% Pi diet.
source: Compared to wild-type mice on normal diet, liver Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 transcript levels were significantly elevated in Col4a3−/− mice but much less elevated on 0.2% Pi (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4C and 4D showing the data.

claim: Excess Pi in Alport mice aggravates inflammation.
source: These data support the notion that excess Pi in Alport mice aggravates inflammation.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the reduction in inflammatory markers with low Pi diet.

claim: Liver Hamp transcript levels were significantly elevated in Col4a3−/− mice compared to wild-type mice on normal diet with complete reversal by low Pi diet.
source: Compared to wild-type mice on normal diet, liver Hamp transcript levels were significantly elevated in Col4a3−/− mice with complete reversal by low Pi diet (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4E showing the data.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet were anemic, with significant reductions in RBC count, MCV, hemoglobin, and serum iron levels.
source: Assessing hematological responses, Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet were anemic, with significant reductions in RBC count, MCV, hemoglobin, and serum iron levels (Figure 4F), as well as in HCT%, MCH, and TSAT% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4F and supplementary figure showing the data.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet displayed profound intracellular iron sequestration in spleen, along with excessive spleen and liver nonheme iron levels.
source: Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet displayed profound intracellular iron sequestration in spleen (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), along with excessive spleen and liver nonheme iron levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4G and supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: Low Pi diet substantially ameliorated hematologic parameters and reduced iron deposits in spleen in Col4a3−/− mice.
source: These effects were substantially ameliorated by low Pi diet in Col4a3−/− mice, with improved hematologic parameters and reduced iron deposits in spleen (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4F and 4G showing the data.

claim: Nonheme iron levels in spleen and liver were reduced in Col4a3−/− mice by low Pi diet treatment, indicating increased iron mobilization and decreased iron restriction.
source: Nonheme iron levels in spleen and liver were reduced in Col4a3−/− mice by treatment, indicating increased iron mobilization and decreased iron restriction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: Dietary Pi restriction improves hematological responses and alleviates hypoferremia.
source: These data indicate that dietary Pi restriction improves hematological responses and alleviates hypoferremia.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in Alport mice on low Pi diet.

claim: Liver Pi levels were increased in Col4a3−/− mice compared to wild-type mice on normal diet and were reduced on low Pi diet.
source: Compared to wild-type mice on normal diet, liver Pi levels were increased in Col4a3−/− mice and were reduced on low Pi diet (Figure 4H).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4H showing the data.

claim: Pi restriction as a dietary intervention, in a genetic model of progressive CKD, reduces pathologic Pi accumulation in the liver and alleviates the severity of renal injury and functional iron deficiency.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that Pi restriction as a dietary intervention, in a genetic model of progressive CKD, reduces pathologic Pi accumulation in the liver and alleviates the severity of renal injury and functional iron deficiency.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in Alport mice on low Pi diet.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice showed significant reduction in grip strength compared to wild-type mice on normal diet which was improved by low Pi diet.
source: Compared to wild-type mice on normal diet, Col4a3−/− mice showed significant reduction in grip strength which was improved by low Pi diet (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5A showing the data.

claim: Gastrocnemius mass was reduced in Col4a3−/− mice, and treatment tended to improve muscle weight.
source: Gastrocnemius mass was also reduced in Col4a3−/− mice, and treatment tended to improve muscle weight (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5B showing the data.

claim: Gastrocnemius Mt1 transcript levels were significantly elevated in Col4a3−/− mice compared to wild-type mice on normal diet and were reduced by low Pi diet.
source: In particular, gastrocnemius Mt1 transcript levels were significantly elevated in Col4a3−/− mice compared to wild-type mice on normal diet and were reduced by low Pi diet (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure showing the data.

claim: Pi restriction as a dietary intervention may improve skeletal muscle abnormalities in CKD.
source: These results suggest that Pi restriction as a dietary intervention may improve skeletal muscle abnormalities in CKD.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in Alport mice on low Pi diet.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice displayed significant elevations in gastrocnemius Mstn transcript levels compared to wild-type mice on normal diet which was reduced by low Pi diet treatment.
source: Furthermore, compared to wild-type mice on normal chow, Col4a3−/− mice displayed significant elevations in gastrocnemius Mstn transcript levels which was reduced by treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5C showing the data.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet showed increased gastrocnemius Murf1 and Atrogin1 transcript levels, which were reduced by low Pi diet.
source: Additionally, Col4a3−/− mice on normal diet showed increased gastrocnemius Murf1 and Atrogin1 transcript levels, which were also reduced by low Pi diet (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5D showing the data.

claim: Dietary Pi restriction, as a treatment in Col4a3−/− mice, reduces myostatin synthesis and subsequent atrophy-related gene programs.
source: These data support the notion that dietary Pi restriction, as a treatment in Col4a3−/− mice, reduces myostatin synthesis and subsequent atrophy-related gene programs.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the gene expression data in Alport mice on low Pi diet.

claim: Gastrocnemius tissue sections from Col4a3−/− mice showed smaller muscle fiber size compared to wild-type controls.
source: As with adenine-induced CKD mice, or mice fed high phosphate diet, gastrocnemius tissue sections from Col4a3−/− mice showed smaller muscle fiber size compared to wild-type controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5E showing the histological data.

claim: Col4a3−/− mice fed low Pi diet showed improved muscle fiber size.
source: However, Col4a3−/− mice fed low Pi diet showed improved muscle fiber size (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 5E showing the histological data.

claim: Hyperphosphatemia affects skeletal muscle wasting in Alport mice, possibly by exacerbating systemic inflammatory cytokine concentrations and their catabolic effects on muscle.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that hyperphosphatemia affects skeletal muscle wasting in Alport mice, possibly by exacerbating systemic inflammatory cytokine concentrations and their catabolic effects on muscle.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in Alport mice, representing an inference from the data.

claim: Primary hepatocytes express high levels of Slc20a1 and Slc20a2 (encoding for PiT-1 and PiT-2), but not Slc17a1 and Slc17a3 (encoding for Npt-1 and Npt-4), or Slc34a1, Slc34a2 and Slc34a3 (encoding for NaPi-2a-c).
source: Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis detected high levels of Slc20a1and Slc20a2 (encoding for PiT-1 and PiT-2), but not Slc17a1 and Slc17a3 (encoding for Npt-1 and Npt-4), or Slc34a1, Slc34a2 and Slc34a3 (encoding for NaPi-2a-c) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figure showing the data.

claim: Type III Na/Pi cotransporters are the predominant Na/Pi family in primary hepatocyte cultures.
source: This analysis indicates that type III Na/Pi cotransporters are the predominant Na/Pi family in primary hepatocyte cultures.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the expression analysis of Na/Pi cotransporters.

claim: Pi treatments increased phosphorylated NFκB levels without changing total NFκB expression in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Immunoblot analysis of ERK1/2, STAT3, and NFκB showed that Pi treatments increased phosphorylated NFκB levels without changing total NFκB expression (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6A showing the immunoblot data.

claim: Increased concentrations of Na2SO4 had no effect on phospho-NFκB levels, indicating the response to elevated Pi was specific and not an unspecific response to increased anions.
source: Increased concentrations of Na2SO4, a salt generating another anionic species, had no effect on phospho-NFκB levels, indicating this response was specific to elevated Pi and not an unspecific response to increased anions.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on the negative control experiment with Na2SO4.

claim: Pi treatment did not affect pERK1/2 or pSTAT3 in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Pi treatment did not affect pERK1/2 or pSTAT3, and FGF23 had no effect on any of the pathways examined.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on the immunoblot analysis.

claim: FGF23 had no effect on ERK1/2, STAT3, or NFκB signaling pathways in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Pi treatment did not affect pERK1/2 or pSTAT3, and FGF23 had no effect on any of the pathways examined.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on the immunoblot analysis.

claim: Elevations in Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 transcript levels were noted following LPS, IL6, and Pi treatments in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Elevations in Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 transcript levels were noted not only following LPS and IL6 but also Pi treatments (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6B and 6C showing the data.

claim: Treatments with Na2SO4 had no effect on Il1b, Il6, and Saa1 gene expression in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Treatments with Na2SO4 had no effect on gene expression.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on the negative control experiment with Na2SO4.

claim: LPS, IL6, and Pi treatments all elevated Hamp transcript levels in cultured hepatocytes.
source: LPS, IL6, and Pi treatments all elevated Hamp transcript levels when compared to control (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6D showing the data.

claim: High extracellular Pi can act on hepatocytes to increase the synthesis of inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin.
source: These data indicate that high extracellular Pi can act on hepatocytes to increase the synthesis of inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the in vitro findings.

claim: Pi significantly increased Slc20a1 transcript levels in a dose-dependent manner in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Expression analysis showed that Pi significantly increased Slc20a1 transcript levels in a dose-dependent manner but had no effect on Slc20a2 expression (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6E and supplementary figure showing the data.

claim: Pi had no effect on Slc20a2 expression in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Expression analysis showed that Pi significantly increased Slc20a1 transcript levels in a dose-dependent manner but had no effect on Slc20a2 expression (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6E and supplementary figure showing the data.

claim: In the presence of PFA, Pi-induced Slc20a1 expression was reduced compared to vehicle-treated control cells.
source: In the presence of PFA, Pi-induced Slc20a1 expression was reduced compared to vehicle-treated control cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6F showing the data.

claim: PFA altered the effects of LPS and IL6 on Slc20a1 expression in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Interestingly, PFA also altered the effects of LPS and IL6 on Slc20a1 expression.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on the PFA cotreatment experiments.

claim: PFA interfered with Pi-induced effects on phospho-NFκB levels without changing total NFκB expression in cultured hepatocytes.
source: To confirm whether inhibiting high extracellular Pi and/or aggregate byproducts disrupts downstream actions of increased extracellular Pi, we cotreated hepatocytes with Pi and PFA, and observed that PFA interfered with Pi-induced effects on phospho-NFκB levels without changing total NFκB expression (Figure 6G, Figure 6—source data 1G).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6G showing the immunoblot data.

claim: The significant elevations in Il1b, Il6, Saa1, and Hamp transcript levels following Pi treatments were reversed in the presence of PFA in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Furthermore, when isolated hepatocytes were treated with either LPS, IL6, or Pi in the presence or absence of PFA, the significant elevations in Il1b, Il6, Saa1, and Hamp transcript levels following Pi treatments were reversed in the presence of PFA (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6H-J showing the data.

claim: PFA slightly altered the effects of LPS on Il6 expression and IL6 on Hamp expression in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Interestingly, PFA slightly altered the effects of LPS on Il6 expression and IL6 on Hamp expression (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 6H-J showing the data.

claim: In primary hepatocyte cultures type III Na/Pi cotransporters are predominant, and increased extracellular Pi activates NFκB signaling, increases PiT-1 expression and induces inflammatory cytokine and hepcidin production.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that in primary hepatocyte cultures type III Na/Pi cotransporters are predominant, and that increased extracellular Pi activates NFκB signaling, increases PiT-1 expression and induces inflammatory cytokine and hepcidin production.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the in vitro findings.

claim: Significant elevations in Il1b, Il6, and Hamp mRNA levels following LPS or Pi treatments were attenuated by BAY 11-7082 in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Significant elevations in Il1b, Il6, and Hamp mRNA levels were detected following LPS or Pi treatments, and these were attenuated by BAY 11-7082 (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 7A and 7B showing the data.

claim: Similar effects of BAY 11-7082 on Saa1, haptoglobin (Hp) and Slc20a1 mRNA expression were observed in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Similar effects of BAY 11-7082 on Saa1, haptoglobin (Hp) and Slc20a1 mRNA expression were also observed, corroborating reports that NFκB directly regulates PiT-1 abundance (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: NFκB directly regulates PiT-1 abundance.
source: Similar effects of BAY 11-7082 on Saa1, haptoglobin (Hp) and Slc20a1 mRNA expression were also observed, corroborating reports that NFκB directly regulates PiT-1 abundance (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript states this as corroboration of existing reports, supported by the BAY 11-7082 data.

claim: Significant elevations in Hamp mRNA levels following LPS or Pi treatments were blunted by addition of anti-IL1β antibody, anti-IL6 antibody, or both neutralizing antibodies in combination in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Expression analysis detected significant elevations in Hamp mRNA levels following LPS or Pi treatments and was blunted by addition of either antibody alone or in combination (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 7C showing the data.

claim: Saa1 and Hp transcript levels were reduced in the presence of anti-IL1β antibody, anti-IL6 antibody, or both in combination, following LPS or Pi treatment in cultured hepatocytes.
source: Compared to vehicle-treated control cells, Saa1 and Hp transcript levels were reduced in the presence of either antibody alone or in combination, following LPS or Pi treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supplementary figures showing the data.

claim: Pi-mediated hepcidin production in cultured hepatocytes is a result of NFκB amplifying PiT-1 expression, which in turn, might intensify high extracellular Pi to augment NFκB regulated inflammatory gene programs, prompting the induction of required cytokines IL1β and IL6 to mediate hepcidin production.
source: Collectively, these results show Pi-mediated hepcidin production in cultured hepatocytes is a result of NFκB amplifying PiT-1 expression, which in turn, might intensify high extracellular Pi to augment NFκB regulated inflammatory gene programs, prompting the induction of required cytokines IL1β and IL6 to mediate hepcidin production.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the in vitro findings with NFκB inhibitor and cytokine neutralization.

claim: Hyperphosphatemia, either as a result of adenine-induced CKD or dietary Pi excess, increases inflammation to exacerbate anemia and skeletal muscle wasting.
source: We report that hyperphosphatemia, either as a result of adenine-induced CKD or dietary Pi excess, increases inflammation to exacerbate anemia and skeletal muscle wasting (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript states this as the main conclusion of the study and references Figure 8 showing a summary diagram.

claim: The complications of hyperphosphatemia are associated with increased liver Pi levels, which correlated with serum Pi concentrations.
source: These complications are associated with increased liver Pi levels, which correlated with serum Pi concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the correlation data from the study.

claim: Supplying a low Pi diet treatment to Alport mice results in beneficial outcomes that reduce functional iron deficiency and skeletal muscle wasting.
source: Supplying a low Pi diet treatment to Alport mice, a genetic model of CKD, results in beneficial outcomes that reduce functional iron deficiency and skeletal muscle wasting.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in Alport mice on low Pi diet.

claim: Pi elevations induce hepatic production of IL6 and IL1β to increase hepcidin expression in hepatocytes, a potential causative link between hyperphosphatemia, anemia, and skeletal muscle dysfunction.
source: Furthermore, our mechanistic in vitro studies indicate that Pi elevations induce hepatic production of IL6 and IL1β to increase hepcidin expression in hepatocytes, a potential causative link between hyperphosphatemia, anemia, and skeletal muscle dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the in vitro mechanistic studies.

claim: On adenine diet, both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice show comparable macroscopic parameters and degrees of functional iron deficiency.
source: Here, we examined wild-type (Fgfr4+/+) and constitutive FGFR4 knockout (Fgfr4−/−) mice subjected to adenine diet or a graded dietary Pi load. We found that on adenine, both Fgfr4+/+ and Fgfr4−/− mice show comparable macroscopic parameters (Table 1) and degrees of functional iron deficiency (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Table 1 and Figure 1 showing the data.

claim: Greater levels of liver Pi in adenine-induced CKD raise the possibility that pathologic Pi deposits, in tissues apart from the vasculature, may contribute to additional complications in CKD.
source: These findings coincide with greater levels of liver Pi, which raises the possibility that pathologic Pi deposits, in tissues apart from the vasculature, may contribute to additional complications in CKD (Komaba and Fukagawa, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states this as a possibility based on the finding of elevated liver Pi, with a citation to support the context.

claim: CKD patients have dysregulated Pi handling.
source: Clinical reports indicate CKD patients have dysregulated Pi handling (Chang et al., 2014; Isakova et al., 2009) and together with the consumption of foods and drinks rich in Pi-based additives, such as in a Westernized diet, extrarenal Pi accumulation may occur (Isakova et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this clinical observation.

claim: Excess Pi leads to depositions into tissues such as the vasculature.
source: A recent study utilizing animal models supports this postulate, demonstrating that excess Pi leads to depositions into tissues such as the vasculature (Zelt et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding.

claim: The major source of body Pi removed during hemodialysis in CKD patients is from cells releasing intracellular Pi.
source: Moreover, a recent report indicates the major source of body Pi removed during hemodialysis in CKD patients, is from cells releasing intracellular Pi (Chazot et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding.

claim: The serum Pi compartment represents a small fraction of total body Pi.
source: As the serum Pi compartment represents a small fraction of total body Pi, and the uptake of excess Pi by tissues is recognized as a detrimental trigger, it is important to examine the degree of pathologic Pi accumulation in nonvascular tissue and whether it exacerbates complications in CKD, such as anemia and muscle wasting.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge to provide context for the study.

claim: No significant changes in macroscopic parameters were observed following dietary Pi overload.
source: In our study, no significant changes in macroscopic parameters were observed following dietary Pi overload (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Table 2 showing the data.

claim: Mice on a 3% Pi diet exhibit increased liver inflammation and Hamp expression, which corroborates previous observation that high dietary Pi influences hepcidin production.
source: However, mice on a 3% Pi diet exhibit increased liver inflammation and Hamp expression, which corroborates previous observation that high dietary Pi influences hepcidin production (Nakao et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and cites a reference to corroborate the observation.

claim: Increased extrarenal Pi accumulation provides a reservoir for storing excess Pi until tissue accumulation achieves saturation, in which case the serum Pi compartment then gradually rises, resulting in hyperphosphatemia.
source: Despite these data suggesting that liver Pi influences liver hepcidin production, our finding might indicate that increased extrarenal Pi accumulation provides a reservoir for storing excess Pi until tissue accumulation achieves saturation, in which case the serum Pi compartment then gradually rises, resulting in hyperphosphatemia.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a possible interpretation of the findings.

claim: Prolonged exposure to Pi, if not maintained in adequate quantities, might trigger pathologic outcomes, as mice on 3% Pi show a noticeable degree of hypoferremia.
source: Furthermore, our data suggest that prolonged exposure to Pi, if not maintained in adequate quantities, might trigger pathologic outcomes, as mice on 3% Pi show a noticeable degree of hypoferremia.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a suggestion based on the findings.

claim: A single intraperitoneal injection of FGF23 blocking peptide was sufficient to rescue anemia in a previous report.
source: However, this work cannot exclude the potential of alternative FGFR isoforms which might mediate the effects of excess FGF23 toward functional iron deficiency following either adenine or 3% Pi diet, as a previous report exhibits the utilization of a single intraperitoneal injection of FGF23 blocking peptide was sufficient to rescue anemia (Agoro et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding from a previous study.

claim: Excess Pi is a hallmark of CKD, but direct pathologic effects of Pi on tissues other than the vasculature are poorly understood.
source: Excess Pi is a hallmark of CKD, but direct pathologic effects of Pi on tissues other than the vasculature are poorly understood (Komaba and Fukagawa, 2016; Scialla and Wolf, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Excess dietary Pi directly exacerbates intestinal inflammation in a model of experimental colitis.
source: Excess dietary Pi was shown to directly exacerbate intestinal inflammation in a model of experimental colitis (Sugihara et al., 2017) and that reducing dietary Pi provides beneficial outcomes toward systemic inflammation, accelerated aging, and survival, as demonstrated in a model of senescence (Morishita et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding from a previous study.

claim: Reducing dietary Pi provides beneficial outcomes toward systemic inflammation, accelerated aging, and survival, as demonstrated in a model of senescence.
source: Excess dietary Pi was shown to directly exacerbate intestinal inflammation in a model of experimental colitis (Sugihara et al., 2017) and that reducing dietary Pi provides beneficial outcomes toward systemic inflammation, accelerated aging, and survival, as demonstrated in a model of senescence (Morishita et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding from a previous study.

claim: CKD illustrates catabolic conditions which are attributable to the vicious cycle generated between mineral dyshomeostasis and inflammation.
source: Inflammatory cytokines can directly target skeletal muscle cells to induce muscle wasting by increasing myostatin production (Zhang et al., 2013), which both together, enhances protein degradation and reduces protein synthesis, as CKD illustrates catabolic conditions which are attributable to the vicious cycle generated between mineral dyshomeostasis and inflammation (Czaya and Faul, 2019b).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about CKD pathophysiology.

claim: Excess Pi influences skeletal muscle dysfunction.
source: This hypothesis is supported by reports demonstrating excess Pi influences skeletal muscle dysfunction (Acevedo et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2020), although it is possible additional FGFR isoforms directly promote skeletal muscle wasting due to excess FGF23 following adenine or high Pi diet.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this finding from previous studies.

claim: FGF23 does not directly affect skeletal muscle dysfunction according to a recent report.
source: However, a recent report suggests that FGF23 does not directly affect skeletal muscle dysfunction (Avin et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding from a previous study.

claim: Hyperphosphatemia, specifically pathologic liver Pi accumulation, rather than pathologic FGF23-FGFR4 signaling, might exacerbate inflammation and hypoferremia.
source: Our data also show liver Pi levels were reduced in Alport mice following low Pi diet treatment, in comparison to Alport mice on normal diet. These findings provide strong evidence that hyperphosphatemia, specifically pathologic liver Pi accumulation, rather than pathologic FGF23-FGFR4 signaling, might exacerbate inflammation and hypoferremia.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings in Alport mice.

claim: The contribution of hyperphosphatemia to skeletal muscle wasting may result from an indirect mechanism that regulates inflammatory cytokines and their pleotropic activities, such as increased liver-derived IL1β and IL6, which might increase overall systemic levels that effectively target skeletal muscle.
source: These findings suggest the contribution of hyperphosphatemia to skeletal muscle wasting may result from an indirect mechanism that regulates inflammatory cytokines and their pleotropic activities, such as increased liver-derived IL1β and IL6, which might increase overall systemic levels that effectively target skeletal muscle.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a suggested mechanism based on the findings.

claim: Elevated Pi concentrations directly affect proximal tubular function.
source: Furthermore, Alport mice on low Pi diet treatment displayed a reduced degree of pathologic kidney function, alterations in kidney morphology, and macroscopic parameters (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 3). Thus, we cannot exclude that these beneficial outcomes in Alport mice observed on treatment may be a repercussion of slightly improved kidney function, as a recent report demonstrates elevated Pi concentrations directly affect proximal tubular function (Shiizaki et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this finding from a recent study.

claim: High extracellular Pi-NFκB signaling axis is observed in vascular smooth muscle cells and ex vivo kidney slices.
source: This high extracellular Pi-NFκB signaling axis is observed in other reservoirs such as vascular smooth muscle cells and ex vivo kidney slices, as well as adjuncts the rewiring of various signaling networks that control cellular homeostasis following excessive Pi exposure (He et al., 2021; Rodríguez-Ortiz et al., 2020; Voelkl et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this finding from previous studies.

claim: Increased liver Pi deposits might underlie a clinical association between elevated body Pi and inflammation.
source: Based on these findings, we speculate increased liver Pi deposits might underlie a clinical association between elevated body Pi and inflammation, where the prolonged duration of tissue accumulation permits Pi in the liver to directly target hepatocytes to induce inflammatory gene programs and hepcidin expression, contributing to hypoferremia.
evidence: The manuscript states this as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Prolonged duration of tissue Pi accumulation permits Pi in the liver to directly target hepatocytes to induce inflammatory gene programs and hepcidin expression, contributing to hypoferremia.
source: Based on these findings, we speculate increased liver Pi deposits might underlie a clinical association between elevated body Pi and inflammation, where the prolonged duration of tissue accumulation permits Pi in the liver to directly target hepatocytes to induce inflammatory gene programs and hepcidin expression, contributing to hypoferremia.
evidence: The manuscript states this as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Associations of inflammation and anemia exist in FTC patients, in addition to patients with and without CKD, before they exhibit hyperphosphatemia.
source: This could explain associations of inflammation and anemia in FTC patients, in addition to patients with and without CKD, before they exhibit hyperphosphatemia (Ramnitz et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2016; Wojcicki, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support these clinical associations.

claim: Clinical studies have demonstrated conflicting outcomes with traditional Pi binders in individuals with nondialysis-dependent CKD.
source: Clinical studies have demonstrated conflicting outcomes with traditional Pi binders in individuals with nondialysis-dependent CKD, but modern Pi binders, such as ferric citrate, demonstrate greater efficacy (Francis et al., 2019; Toussaint et al., 2020), and are being evaluated for their effect on CKD comorbidities.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about clinical studies.

claim: Modern Pi binders, such as ferric citrate, demonstrate greater efficacy than traditional Pi binders.
source: Clinical studies have demonstrated conflicting outcomes with traditional Pi binders in individuals with nondialysis-dependent CKD, but modern Pi binders, such as ferric citrate, demonstrate greater efficacy (Francis et al., 2019; Toussaint et al., 2020), and are being evaluated for their effect on CKD comorbidities.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about clinical studies.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of type II Na/Pi cotransporters holds potential for therapeutic actions.
source: Treatments, such as pharmacologic inhibition of type II Na/Pi cotransporters, hold potential for therapeutic actions (Clerin et al., 2020; Thomas et al., 2019) but do not aim at altered mineral metabolism.
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this statement about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: Anti-FGFR4 therapy may be beneficial toward cardiomyopathy.
source: Moreover, as studies indicate anti-FGFR4 therapy may be beneficial toward cardiomyopathy (Grabner et al., 2015), our data suggest these same beneficial outcomes for inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting would not apply.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this statement about anti-FGFR4 therapy.

claim: Anti-FGFR4 therapy would not provide beneficial outcomes for inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting based on the current study's data.
source: Moreover, as studies indicate anti-FGFR4 therapy may be beneficial toward cardiomyopathy (Grabner et al., 2015), our data suggest these same beneficial outcomes for inflammation, anemia, and skeletal muscle wasting would not apply.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the findings that FGFR4 knockout did not protect against these complications.

claim: The study features a possibility to improve CKD patient survival and specific rare genetic disorders, such as FTC, by limiting excess body Pi.
source: Altogether, our study features a possibility to improve CKD patient survival and specific rare genetic disorders, such as FTC, by limiting excess body Pi.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion about the potential clinical implications of the study.
